title: Is Instant Coffee Bad For Your Health?
summary: Is instant coffee bad for you? Instant has less caffeine and no cafestol, but acrylamide runs higher and sugary 3-in-1 mixes are the real risk.
body_markdown:
Instant coffee takes mere seconds: stir a spoonful of crystals into a mug and you're out the door before a drip machine would have finished gurgling. That speed makes some people wonder whether they're giving something up for it. If you've ever searched "instant coffee bad for health," you've probably run into warnings about acrylamide (a compound that forms when some foods, including coffee beans, are roasted), processing and sugary sachets.


So does that quick mug actually cost you anything? In this article, we compare instant with brewed coffee on acrylamide, caffeine and cholesterol, and we look at what goes into those sweetened 3-in-1 sachets.


## Is instant coffee bad for you? The short answer


No. Plain instant coffee is a reasonable daily choice, provided you read the label and pick a quality product. Here's how it compares with brewed coffee:


-


**Acrylamide:** Instant powder often runs about two to three times higher than roasted ground coffee in the surveys cited below, though results vary. Estimates for a 2 g serving are about 0.72–1.42 µg.


-


**Caffeine:** A typical cup of instant has slightly less caffeine than brewed, about 62 mg versus 96 mg per 8 oz.


-


**Antioxidants:** Instant retains chlorogenic acids, the main antioxidant family in coffee.


-


**Cholesterol:** Instant and filtered coffee contain negligible cafestol, the compound that raises LDL cholesterol.


-


**The real caveat:** 3-in-1 sachets add sugar, glucose syrup and creamers made with palm kernel oil.


## What is instant coffee?


Instant coffee is brewed coffee with the water taken out. Manufacturers brew roasted beans into a concentrated extract, then dry it into crystals or powder that dissolve completely when you add water. You'll also see it called soluble coffee. A standard cup uses about 2 g of powder, roughly a teaspoon, in 5–6 fl oz of water (about two-thirds of a cup). Nothing gets left behind in a filter, which explains several of the health differences below.


## How instant coffee is made


Manufacturers dry the coffee extract with one of two methods, and that choice can affect flavor, cost and some of the chemistry in your cup.


### Spray-drying vs freeze-drying


Spray-drying uses hot air, and freeze-drying uses cold and a vacuum.


-


**Spray-drying:** Manufacturers mist coffee extract into a chamber of hot air, and the droplets dry into fine powder.


-


**Freeze-drying:** Manufacturers freeze the extract, then the ice turns straight to vapor under vacuum. The product has to stay a few degrees below the point where its structure would collapse.


From a health perspective, neither method has a clear edge. In[one soluble coffee study](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2772275922000090) , spray-freeze-dried powder held 52.35 mg chlorogenic acids per gram against 49.89 for freeze-dried, but overall, the data on antioxidant retention are mixed.


### Why processing changes the chemistry


Instant coffee starts as roasted beans, so it inherits whatever formed during roasting, acrylamide included. Concentrating and drying the brew leaves those roast compounds in a smaller, denser package.


Soluble coffee contains negligible cafestol and kahweol, the oily compounds that raise cholesterol. Caffeine remains in the finished product, and the amount per cup depends on how much powder you use.


## Acrylamide in instant coffee: how worried should you be?


Acrylamide is a compound that forms when coffee beans are roasted. Animal studies link it to cancer, so food safety agencies keep an eye on it.


Instant powder usually carries more of it than roasted ground coffee. EFSA's[2016 report](https://www.efsa.europa.eu/sites/default/files/corporate_publications/files/161215chemicalsinfoodreport.pdf) found roasted coffee almost three times lower than instant.


The amount in your cup is small. A typical cup uses about 1 teaspoon (2 g) of powder. That works out to roughly 0.72–1.42 µg of acrylamide, assuming all of it ends up in the cup. It's around 2–5% of an average adult's daily acrylamide from all foods. Coffee overall accounts for 34% of average adult exposure, and fried potato products for up to 49%.


Worth noting: The FDA's consumer advice doesn't tell you to stop drinking coffee. Your cup of instant is a small slice of the picture, and your overall eating plan matters more.

### Caffeine per cup


Instant coffee usually has less caffeine per cup than drip coffee. An 8 oz cup of instant averages about 62 mg, against about 96 mg for brewed. Instant decaf comes in at about 2 mg.


Instant powder carries roughly 18–44 mg of caffeine per gram. A typical cup uses about 2 g of powder, so you land around 36–88 mg depending on the brand. Instant varies more from cup to cup than brewed coffee, because the dose depends on how much powder goes in.


If you track caffeine, level your spoon and use the same mug. Of everything in this section, that's the factor you control most directly.


### Antioxidants and chlorogenic acids


Instant coffee keeps its chlorogenic acids, which are major antioxidant compounds in coffee.


Chlorogenic acids are the main family of polyphenols, plant compounds with antioxidant activity, in coffee beans. They shape coffee's flavor and much of its antioxidant activity.


Instant coffee keeps them. One product survey found roughly 9–54 mg in a serving of plain instant. No study has measured instant and brewed coffee side by side with the same method, so a clean comparison isn't available.


Roasting breaks some chlorogenic acids down, so a lighter roast keeps more.


### Cholesterol: where instant wins


Instant coffee has negligible cafestol and kahweol, two oily compounds from the bean's own oils. These compounds raise LDL, the "bad" cholesterol, so instant skips the LDL-raising effect of unfiltered coffee. A paper filter traps them. A French press or boiling pot lets them through.


The human trials back this up:


-


**Purified cafestol:** In a[randomized crossover trial of 10 healthy men](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9022539) , 61–64 mg a day for 28 days raised LDL by 0.57 mmol/L (22 mg/dL).


-


**Dose-response:** Every 10 mg of cafestol a day raises total cholesterol by about 0.13 mmol/L (5 mg/dL).


-


**Pooled trials:** A[2001 meta-analysis](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11207153) found unfiltered coffee raises total and LDL cholesterol. Filtered coffee showed very little increase.


### Acidity and stomach tolerance


Nobody has published a pH reading for brewed instant coffee, so "instant is less acidic" is unproven.


Caffeine seems to matter more than acidity. In one[older study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7002705) , instant coffee lowered pressure in the valve between stomach and esophagus (the food pipe). It did so whether the coffee was adjusted to pH 4.5 or pH 7.0. pH is a measure of acidity, and 7.0 is neutral. Another study found[decaffeination significantly reduced coffee-induced reflux](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7918922) .


If coffee bothers your stomach, these simple changes are worth a go, though none is a proven reflux remedy:


-


Switch to decaf instant, which has about 2 mg caffeine per cup.


-


Use a smaller serving of powder.


-


Add a splash of creamer to mellow the sharp, acidic taste of the cup. Our coconut-based[Superfood Creamer](https://lairdsuperfood.com/collections/laird-superfood-creamers) stirs straight into instant coffee, so you'll notice a smoother, creamier sip.


## The real problem: sugar, creamer and 3-in-1 mixes


Sweetened sachets bring added sugar and creamer into your cup. Most 3-in-1 mix pairs instant coffee with sugar and a non-dairy creamer. In many mixes, that creamer is glucose syrup, hydrogenated (chemically hardened) palm kernel or coconut oil, and sodium caseinate, a milk protein.


The numbers add up quickly. A single 3-in-1 sachet can carry up to about 18 g of sugar, or roughly 4 teaspoons. It can also carry up to about 5 g of saturated fat from the creamer. Two sachets in a day can mean up to about 37 g of sugar, or roughly 9 teaspoons.


Creamers made with partially hydrogenated oils can also carry trans fats. That is a separate concern from sugar and saturated fat.


Population research on heavy mix drinking is mixed. Some studies find higher odds of metabolic syndrome (a cluster of risk factors for heart disease and diabetes), while others find lower odds or no link. These studies capture one moment in time, so they can't show cause and effect. None of it points at plain instant coffee.


What you can act on is the label. Check the sugar and saturated fat per sachet. If you like a creamy cup, plain instant plus a creamer you choose gives you control over both sugar and fat.


## How much instant coffee per day is safe?


For most healthy adults, up to 400 mg of caffeine a day is the line recommended by the FDA. At about 62 mg per 8 oz cup, 400 mg works out to roughly six cups of instant. Because brands range from 18 to 44 mg per gram, a strong spoonful brings that number down.


Check in with your health practitioner if you're pregnant, breastfeeding or planning a pregnancy. The same goes if caffeine is on the table for a child or teen, if you take medications, or if it leaves you jittery or keeps you up at night.


Count every source toward your total, including tea, cola and energy drinks.


## How to choose the healthiest instant coffee


The healthiest instant coffee is plain coffee with nothing hiding in it. Here's what to check on the label and how our lineup compares:


-


**Plain or unsweetened:** You add your own sugar and creamer, or skip them.


-


**Certified organic:** Look for the certification on the label if organic beans matter to you.


-


**A short real-food list:** On a plain jar, coffee should be the only entry or close to it.


-


**No seed oils or hydrogenated oils:** These show up in the creamer portion of many mixes.


-


**Named added real food:** Look for each add-in listed by name, not tucked into a proprietary blend.


-


**A decaf or lower-caffeine option:** This helps if you're sensitive, pregnant or drinking late in the day.

## FAQ


These answers cover acrylamide, caffeine, sweetened mixes, antioxidants, acidity, cholesterol and choosing your daily amount.


### Is acrylamide in instant coffee dangerous at normal intake?


A typical cup of instant, about 1 teaspoon (2 g) of powder, works out to roughly 0.72–1.42 µg of acrylamide. That's around 2–5% of an average adult's daily acrylamide from all foods.


### Does instant coffee have less caffeine than brewed?


Usually, yes. An 8 oz cup of instant averages about 62 mg, against about 96 mg for brewed. Instant varies widely by brand and spoon size, from about 18 to 44 mg per gram of powder.


### Are 3-in-1 coffee mixes healthy?


They're the weak spot in the lineup of instant coffee products. A single sachet can carry up to about 18 g of sugar (roughly 4 teaspoons) and up to about 5 g of saturated fat. The creamers often contain glucose syrup and hydrogenated palm kernel oil. Population research on heavy mix drinking is mixed and can't show cause and effect.


### Does instant coffee still have antioxidants?


Yes. Instant keeps chlorogenic acids. These are the main family of plant compounds with antioxidant activity in coffee. No study has compared instant and brewed coffee side by side with the same method.


### Is instant coffee less acidic than brewed?


No published study has measured the pH (a measure of acidity) of brewed instant coffee. Generally, measures taken to reduce the effects of coffee on stomach acid are applicable to both brewed and instant coffee.


### What's the healthiest type of instant coffee?


Look for plain, certified organic coffee with a short label and no seed or hydrogenated oils, like Laird Superfood[Instant Functional Coffees](https://lairdsuperfood.com/collections/functional-instant-coffees) . Choose a decaf or lower-caffeine version if you're sensitive, like[Mushroom Coffee](https://lairdsuperfood.com/products/mushroom-instant-coffee?variant=44049994612771) or[Electrolyte Coffee](https://lairdsuperfood.com/collections/electrolyte-coffee) .


### Is instant coffee better than French press for cholesterol?


Yes. Instant has negligible cafestol, an oily compound in coffee, while boiled and French press coffee carry several milligrams per cup. Cafestol raises LDL ("bad") cholesterol in human trials, at about 0.13 mmol/L (a standard blood-test unit) total cholesterol per 10 mg a day.


### How many cups of instant coffee a day is safe?


Most healthy adults can stay within 400 mg of caffeine, roughly six cups of instant at 62 mg each.
